carousel.title: 1. Overview
carousel.heading: $500,000 raised in half the projected fundraising window
carousel.content:
Valet Vault, LLC - Atlanta, GA - 2020

A parking industry founder had a patent-pending product, a manufacturing partner, and no investor documentation. We had 17 days to build the financial model, executive summary, and pitch deck from scratch - including a strategic recommendation to reposition the company from a hardware business to a hardware-plus-SaaS model. The client raised $500,000 - double the $250,000 goal - in half the projected fundraising window.

carousel.title: 2. Details
carousel.heading: 17 days, $5,500 fixed fee, $500K seed round
carousel.content:
- Engagement fee: $5,500 fixed fee
- Timeline: 17 days (April 17-May 4, 2020)
- Capital raised: $500,000 seed round
- Fundraising goal: $250,000 (2x exceeded)
- Projected company valuation: $12M (5x FY22 EBITDA)
- Equity offered: 5% at $5M valuation - 59.3% discount to modeled current value
- Client type: Hardware/SaaS startup, valet station equipment, pre-revenue
- Status: Funded and launched

carousel.title: 3. The Situation
carousel.heading: A real product with no investor infrastructure
carousel.content:
Zach Wojohn had spent 25 years in the valet parking industry. He'd built one of Atlanta's largest parking management companies from scratch and had a clear-eyed view of the problem: the valet podium - the physical station where operators secure customer car keys - hadn't changed meaningfully in two decades. The equipment was flimsy, insecure, and had no technology layer. He'd designed a better one. His manufacturing partner, Henry INC, had the floor space and fabrication capability to build it. The product was real.

What didn't exist was anything an investor would need to say yes. There was no financial model, no valuation methodology, no projection of how the business would scale, and no document that could walk a seed investor through the opportunity in a structured way. The founder had product cost data and pricing assumptions, but nothing that connected those inputs to a five-year business case.

There was also a strategic gap neither party had fully named yet. The original concept was hardware-only - sell the Defender podium, collect revenue per unit. The product's smart-lock and access-monitoring technology pointed toward something more valuable: a recurring SaaS revenue layer that would change what the company was worth at exit. That insight was sitting in the product specs. It needed someone to build it into the model.

carousel.title: 4. The Ask
carousel.heading: Investor materials, model logic, valuation, and strategic repositioning
carousel.content:
The client needed investor materials. What the work actually required was different:

- A ground-up financial model with documented assumptions - not a spreadsheet, but a fully variable pro forma that could survive scrutiny from outside accountants
- A business model recommendation: evaluate whether the hardware-only structure was the right go-forward model or whether a SaaS layer should be built in from the start
- A company valuation derived from the model, with a defensible methodology
- An equity offer structure that gave investors a clear, time-sensitive reason to act
- An executive summary that read as a mini business plan - specific enough for a sophisticated investor, accessible enough for a first conversation
- A pitch deck that worked in tandem with the summary as a live presentation vehicle

carousel.title: 5. The Approach
carousel.heading: Model first, then build the investor story from the numbers
carousel.content:
The first decision was sequencing. The financial model had to come before everything else - not because it was the most visible deliverable, but because every other document depended on it. The executive summary's market analysis, the investor offer terms, the valuation, the go-to-market strategy - none of that could be written with credibility until we knew what the numbers actually said. We built the model first, let the assumptions settle, and wrote everything else from that foundation.

The second decision was the SaaS recommendation. The Defender's smart-lock technology had a web-based access and monitoring platform planned as a companion product. We looked at the margin structure: hardware units had a fixed production cost of $2,602 against a base retail of $5,199. The SaaS subscriptions - priced from $69.95 to $199.95 per month - carried near-zero incremental production cost once the platform was built. A hardware business is valued on revenue multiples. A SaaS business is valued on recurring revenue multiples. Building the SaaS trajectory into the model from Year 1 changed what the company was worth at every point in the projection. We made that recommendation early and built the entire financial architecture around it.

The go-to-market strategy followed the same logic: don't compete on price, compete on category. The Defender was priced above every competitor. That meant the marketing job wasn't to sell a better podium - it was to make "podium security" a concept the industry took seriously enough to pay a premium for. We structured the strategy around two third-party credibility levers - a UL burglary rating and a parking insurance underwriter endorsement - rather than advertising spend. Both would cost time, not money, and would create durable positioning that competitors couldn't easily replicate.

carousel.title: 6. The Work
carousel.heading: Pro forma, valuation, executive summary, GTM strategy, and pitch deck
carousel.content:
Pro Forma Financial Model
A fully variable, assumption-backed five-year model covering FY2021 through FY2025 with quarterly breakdowns. Built five independent revenue streams - hardware sales, upgrade customizations, technology add-ons, maintenance services, and SaaS subscriptions - each with its own cost structure, growth rate, and margin profile. Key assumptions: 8% quarterly sales growth, SaaS attach rate beginning at 15% of monthly unit sales in Q3 FY2021 and scaling to 56% by FY2022, SaaS representing 35% of gross by Year 3. The model was reviewed by outside accountants retained by an investor and required no material revision.

Company Valuation and Equity Structure
Derived a $12M current valuation using a 5x FY22 EBITDA multiple - the standard methodology for a product-asset business with $1M+ annual gross. Structured the initial $250K angel investment at 5% equity priced against a $5M valuation, representing a 59.3% discount to the modeled current value. The discount-to-value framing was deliberate: it gave investors a concrete, defensible reason to act without requiring a hard deadline.

Executive Summary
A 27-page investor document covering product introduction, company overview, multi-stream business model architecture, market analysis sourced from a purchased 2020 AnythingResearch Premium Report on Parking Lots & Garages (registered to this engagement), competitive analysis against Valet Spot and SD2K, SWOT analysis, go-to-market strategy, full projected income statements, and investor offer with equity distribution. Written to function as a mini business plan - specific enough for due diligence, readable in a single sitting.

Go-to-Market Strategy
Two-lever positioning approach built around third-party validation rather than marketing spend. Lever one: pursue a UL burglary rating to reframe the Defender from operational equipment to security imperative - a category shift that eliminates price objections. Lever two: seek endorsement from a parking insurance underwriter, an unprecedented move that would create industry-level best-practice validation no competitor could match.

Pitch Deck
A companion investor presentation designed to work in tandem with the executive summary - the summary as a leave-behind, the deck as the live meeting vehicle. Structured to walk a seed investor from market context to product differentiation to financial model to investor offer in a single presentation sequence.

carousel.title: 7. The Impact
carousel.heading: $500K raised, target doubled, accountant review passed
carousel.content:
Materials produced and engagement completed on schedule within the 17-day project window.

- $500,000 raised - double the $250,000 fundraising goal
- Closed in half the projected fundraising timeline
- Financial model survived outside accountant review - the investor retained independent accountants; the model required no material revision
- Unsolicited job offer extended to the engagement consultant by a reviewing investor, based on the quality of the financial model
- Business model repositioned from hardware-only to hardware-plus-SaaS, with SaaS projected at 35% of gross revenue by Year 3 at zero additional production cost
- [PROJECTION - not yet realized at time of engagement] Five-year net income trajectory from $1.16M (FY2021) to $10.0M (FY2025) per modeled assumptions

carousel.title: 8. The Deliverables
carousel.heading: A full investor-readiness package delivered in 17 days
carousel.content:
- Pro Forma Financial Model - A fully variable five-year model with documented assumptions, five independent revenue streams, quarterly income statements, and a SaaS ramp schedule; built to survive investor due diligence
- Company Valuation Memo - A 5x EBITDA methodology producing a $12M current value, embedded in the executive summary's investor offer section
- Equity Offer Structure - A $250K angel investment at 5% equity priced at a 59.3% discount to modeled current value, designed to create investor urgency without a hard close deadline
- Executive Summary - A 27-page investor document functioning as a mini business plan: market analysis, competitive landscape, SWOT, business model architecture, financial projections, and investor offer
- Pitch Deck - A 10-25 slide investor presentation aligned to the executive summary, designed as the live-meeting complement to the leave-behind document
- Go-to-Market Strategy - A two-lever positioning framework built around UL burglary rating pursuit and insurance underwriter endorsement, designed to reframe the product category rather than compete on price
- Statement of Work - A signed, milestone-based consulting agreement defining scope, three-stage payment schedule, and delivery dates; executed on time at all three milestones
